An annotation is a note, comment, or explanation that is added to a piece of existing content — such as a book, a document, an image, a piece of code, or a dataset — in order to explain, clarify, describe, or add information about that content.

The single most important thing to understand about the word is this: an annotation is always secondary. It is never the original content. It is something that gets layered on top of or alongside the original, without replacing or altering it. The original content exists first; the annotation comes after, as an addition.

Imagine you are reading a history textbook. You come across a sentence that mentions "The Treaty of Versailles" but doesn't explain what it is. Your teacher has already read this book and written a short note in the margin: "This was the peace agreement signed in 1919 after World War I."

That note in the margin is an annotation. It doesn't change what the book says. It simply sits beside the original text and gives you more information to help you understand it.

That is the essence of an annotation — a helpful addition attached to something, pointing at something specific within it, and saying more about it.

Annotations exist to serve several related purposes, and understanding these helps you grasp the full weight of the word:

To explain or clarify. When a part of the original content is difficult, technical, or ambiguous, an annotation breaks it down into simpler terms. A footnote at the bottom of a legal document that explains what a complicated clause means is an annotation doing this job.

To provide context. Sometimes the original content is clear on its own, but knowing the background makes it richer or more useful. A note attached to a historical photograph that reads "Taken during the Great Depression, 1932, New York City" is giving context. That note is an annotation.

To label or categorize. In some fields, especially in science and technology, annotations are used to tag or label specific things so that others can find, sort, or understand them easily. A scientist might annotate a gene in a genome sequence to indicate what that gene does.

To express a reaction, critique, or opinion. A reader who writes "I disagree with this argument" next to a paragraph in a book is annotating it — adding their own perspective as a note tied to that specific part of the text.

To cross-reference. An annotation might point you toward another source, saying in effect: "If you want to learn more about this, see page 47" or "Compare this with Chapter 5."
Where you encounter annotations in everyday life

The concept shows up in many different places, and recognizing it across these contexts is important:

In books and printed texts. This is the oldest and most familiar form. Annotations in books are the handwritten or printed notes found in margins (called marginal notes), at the bottom of a page (footnotes), or at the end of a chapter or book (endnotes). When a book is published with expert notes already built in — to help readers understand a difficult classic, for example — it is called an annotated edition or annotated version. The annotations in such a book might explain old words, historical references, or cultural context that a modern reader might not know.

In digital documents. When you use a program like Google Docs, Microsoft Word, or a PDF reader and you leave a comment on a specific part of the text, you are creating an annotation. The original document stays unchanged; your comment floats beside it, attached to the exact spot you highlighted.

In code (programming). Programmers routinely add short notes within their code to explain what different sections do. These are called annotations (or sometimes "comments," a word used interchangeably in this context). They are meant for other programmers — or for the same programmer returning to the code later — and are typically ignored by the computer when the code runs.

In science and research. Scientists annotate diagrams, images, and data constantly. A labeled diagram of the human heart — with arrows pointing to each part and the name written beside it — is an annotated diagram. Each label is an annotation.

In machine learning and artificial intelligence. This is a modern and increasingly important use. Before an AI can learn to recognize objects in photos or understand spoken language, humans must go through thousands of images or recordings and label them. A person who looks at a photo and types "this is a cat" is annotating that image. This process is called data annotation, and it is how AI systems are trained.

In law and official documents. Legal texts are often dense and hard to understand. Annotations are added — sometimes by publishers, sometimes by legal experts — to explain what each clause means, how courts have interpreted it, and what its practical effects are. A heavily annotated legal code is a common reference tool for lawyers.
What makes an annotation distinct from a simple "note"

This is a subtle but important distinction. A note is a general word — it can stand entirely on its own, independent of anything else. A shopping list, a diary entry, a reminder you wrote to yourself — these are all notes.

An annotation, however, is always attached to and dependent upon something else. It cannot exist in isolation in a meaningful way, because its entire purpose is to refer to, explain, or add information about a specific piece of existing content. Detach an annotation from what it is annotating and it often loses its meaning. The annotation "This refers to the 1814 battle" means nothing by itself — you need to know what "this" is pointing to.

So the key difference is one of attachment and dependency: an annotation always belongs to something; a note can stand alone.
A note on the difference between "annotation" and "comment"

In many everyday contexts, these two words are used interchangeably, and that is perfectly acceptable. However, "annotation" tends to carry a slightly more formal, deliberate, or scholarly tone. When someone says "I added a comment," it can feel casual and spontaneous. When someone says "I added an annotation," it suggests a more intentional act — typically one meant to inform, explain, or enrich the content it is attached to, often in a structured or systematic way.

In technical fields like software engineering or data science, the two words sometimes have distinct, precise meanings defined by the tools being used — but in general language, they overlap heavily.

An annotation is any note, label, explanation, or comment that is deliberately added to an existing piece of content — text, image, code, data, or otherwise — in order to explain, clarify, contextualize, label, or enrich that content. It is always secondary to the original; it adds to it without replacing it. It is always attached to something specific within the original content, pointing at it and saying something more about it. You encounter annotations in books, digital documents, scientific diagrams, legal texts, programming code, and AI training data. The act of creating annotations is called annotating, and a piece of content that has had annotations added to it is described as annotated.
